items.problem: Korean counts things with counters: '폭탄 세 개가' not '세 폭탄이', and '25명을' not '25 사람을'. '하나가' also needs '그중' to carry the English 'one [of them]'. Item 10 of the same file repeats '세 폭탄이'.
items.correction: 폭탄 세 개가 폭발했고, 그중 하나가 25명을 다치게 했다.  (item 10 → '폭탄 세 개가 폭발해서 세 사람이 죽었다.')

items.original: 나는 영어를 공부해왔다(한 적이 있다, 다했다).
items.problem: The third gloss is meant to be the 완료 sense of the present perfect, i.e. '다 했다' (finished doing it), but written solid as '다했다' it is the verb '다하다' (to be exhausted / to run out), which is a different word. Item 13 of the same file has '나는 한 때 영어를 공부한 적이 있다.' where '한 때' should be the single word '한때'.
items.correction: item 15 → '나는 영어를 공부해왔다(한 적이 있다, 다 했다).'; item 13 → '나는 한때 영어를 공부한 적이 있다.'

items.original: "n": "25", "text": "I didn't see any person.", "alternatives": ["I didn't see anyone."]
items.problem: The Korean is "나는 어떤 사람도 보지 않았다." "anybody" is as standard as "anyone" here, but it is missing from the alternatives and the grader does not treat the two as the same word: the shipped grader scores "I didn't see anybody." as incorrect (0). ("I didn't see any person." is also the least natural of the three and is the one shown as the model answer.)
items.correction: Add the alternatives "I didn't see anybody." and "I saw no one.", and consider promoting "I didn't see anyone." to the model answer.

items.locator: item 10 — Korean prompt (gh2-017-1 items[].text #10) against English "Back home, he had a family to support."
items.original: 뒤쪽 고향에 그는 부양할 가족이 있었다.
items.problem: "Back home" here means 고향에서는 / 고국에서는; "뒤쪽 고향에" ('at the rear hometown') comes from glossing 'back' as 뒤쪽 and is not Korean. Unlike the other literal glosses in this course, this item has no natural reading in parentheses, so nothing corrects it.
items.correction: Change to "고향에서는 그에게 부양할 가족이 있었다." (natural gloss optional: "고국에 남겨둔 부양가족이 있었다").

items.original: "n": "15", "text": "Either is good.", "alternatives": ["Either one is good.", "Anything is good."]
items.problem: "Anything is good." is not equivalent to "Either is good." — 'either' is restricted to one of TWO, which is exactly the point of this block (items 11-16: the two / both / neither / either / nothing). Alternatives are displayed to the learner as "다른 정답: …" (GrammarLearningView.tsx:915-917), so the page presents the wrong equivalence as a correct answer.
items.correction: Remove the alternative "Anything is good." and make the two-item scope explicit in the Korean prompt: "어느 것이나 좋다." → "둘 중 어느 것이든 좋다."

items.locator: item 16 — Korean prompt (gh2-017-1 items[].text #16) against English "Nothing is good."
items.original: 어느 것도 좋지 않다.
items.problem: This prompt is the same wording as item 14 ("둘 중 어느 것도 좋지 않다." = Neither is good.) minus "둘 중", and it reads most naturally as none/neither rather than 'nothing'. Item 16 has no alternatives, so the shipped grader scores "None is good." incorrect (0) and "Neither is good." incorrect (0).
items.correction: Change the Korean to "아무것도 좋지 않다." and add the alternatives "None is good." and "None of them is good."

items.locator: blocks[] paragraph block between item 13 and item 14 (English page)
items.original: The plan was opposed by the members.
items.problem: A real teaching sentence — the passive counterpart of item 13 — is stored as a paragraph block instead of a sentence item, and paragraph blocks are never rendered (GrammarLearningView builds items only from 'sentences' blocks, GrammarLearningView.tsx:156-167; LessonBody returns the grammar view before any paragraph renderer). The oppose/be opposed contrast the lesson sets up is therefore invisible.
items.correction: Either promote it to a numbered item with a Korean prompt in gh2-018-1 ("그 계획은 회원들에 의해 반대되었다."), which changes the item count on both pages, or delete the dead block.

items.original: "n": "12", "text": "You've changed much since I saw you last.", "alternatives": ["You've changed a lot since I saw you last."]
items.problem: As a degree adverb in an affirmative statement, bare 'much' is formal/literary in modern English; the ordinary form is "a lot", which is already the alternative.
items.correction: Make "You've changed a lot since I saw you last." the model answer and keep the 'much' version as the alternative.

items.original: I took her by the arm**s**.  (exact JSON: {"n": "17", "text": "I took her by the arms."})
items.problem: The fixed idiom taught by every learner dictionary is "take/grab/hold someone BY THE ARM" (singular) — Longman and Oxford give "She took him by the arm and pushed him out of the door". The plural "by the arms" is a different, unusual image, and the Korean prompt is the singular "나는 그녀의 팔을 잡았다." There is no alternative, so the standard idiom is penalised: the shipped grader scores "I took her by the arm." as partial (70 points), not exact.
items.correction: Make "I took her by the arm." the model answer and keep "I took her by the arms." as an alternative (or drop it).

items.locator: item 23 — Korean prompt (gh2-018-1 items[].text #23) against English "A conference was held."
items.original: 한 대회가 열렸다.
items.problem: "대회" in ordinary Korean means a competition/tournament/rally; "conference" is 회의 (or 학술대회 when academic). The prompt therefore points the learner at the wrong English word, and there is no alternative: the shipped grader scores "A competition was held." as incorrect (0).
items.correction: Change the Korean to "한 회의가 열렸다." (or "회의가 개최되었다."), and/or add alternatives "A meeting was held." / "A conference took place."

items.locator: item 17 — Korean prompt (gh2-019-1 items[].text #17) against English "How do you keep in shape?"
items.original: 어떻게 너는 모습 속에 (적절한 몸매를)유지하나?(혹은, 건강을 유지하니?)
items.problem: The literal part is not parsable Korean: "모습 속에 … 유지하나" is a word-by-word rendering of "in shape" that has no meaning in Korean, the object marker is stranded inside a parenthesis, and there is no space before 유지하나. The item then offers two different natural readings in parentheses, so the learner is left with one broken sentence and two competing glosses.
items.correction: Replace with a single clean prompt: "너는 어떻게 몸매(건강)를 유지하니?"

items.original: Americans don't eat fish raw.
items.problem: Presented as a current fact about a nationality, this is false today: raw fish is mainstream in the US. IBISWorld puts US sushi-restaurant revenue at about $33.2 billion in 2025 with roughly 4,000 sushi restaurants; poke and sashimi are also common. The sentence also teaches a national stereotype rather than the grammar point (목적격보어 'raw'), which any neutral subject would carry.
items.correction: Replace the subject/claim while keeping the 5형식 pattern, e.g. "Some people don't eat fish raw." / "He doesn't eat fish raw." with Korean "어떤 사람들은 생선을 날로 먹지 않는다." If the original sentence is kept for archival reasons, it must not be presented as a fact about Americans today.

items.locator: item 1 — Korean prompt (gh2-021-1 items[].text #1) against English "The President appointed him his secretary."
items.original: 그 대통령은 그를 그의 비서(장관)으로 임명했다.
items.problem: In "appointed him HIS secretary" the word means a personal secretary (비서); a cabinet secretary (장관) is never "his secretary" but "Secretary of State/Defense". The parenthetical 장관 therefore offers a reading the English sentence cannot have. (The particle is also wrong for 비서: 비서로, not 비서(장관)으로.)
items.correction: Change to "그 대통령은 그를 자신의 비서로 임명했다."

items.original: "n": "13", "text": "Let me make you amends for your loss.", "alternatives": ["Let me make amends to you for your loss."]
items.problem: "make amends" is a fixed phrase that takes 'to someone for something'; the ditransitive "make you amends" is archaic and effectively unused in modern English. The alternative already carries the standard form.
items.correction: Make "Let me make amends to you for your loss." the model answer and keep the ditransitive as the alternative if the 4형식 point must be shown.

items.original: What kind of a king will he make?
items.problem: "What kind of a king…" is the older, criticised form; the form taught and used today is "What kind of king will he make?" The item has no alternatives, so the modern standard answer is penalised — the shipped grader scores "What kind of king will he make?" as partial (70), not exact.
items.correction: Add the alternative "What kind of king will he make?" (preferably as the model answer, keeping the "kind of a" variant as an alternative).

items.locator: item 22 (items[].text + alternatives, English page; Korean gh2-021-1 #22 "나는 나 자신이 유죄라고 느꼈다.")
items.original: "n": "22", "text": "I felt myself guilty.", "alternatives": ["I felt guilty."]
items.problem: Two problems in one item. (1) "I felt myself guilty." is not natural English; the 5형식 pattern with 'feel' needs a participle or clause ("I felt myself growing tired", "I felt that I was guilty"). (2) The Korean "나 자신이 유죄라고 느꼈다" says legal guilt (유죄), but the accepted alternative "I felt guilty." means 죄책감을 느꼈다 — the two accepted answers do not mean the same thing.
items.correction: Make "I felt guilty." the model answer with Korean "나는 죄책감을 느꼈다."; if the 5형식 point must be kept, use a well-formed example such as "I found myself guilty." or "I felt that I was guilty." and match the Korean to it.

items.locator: blocks[] paragraph block between the two sentences blocks (Korean page, after item 16)
items.original: 미국 사람은 네꺼 내꺼 철저히 따진다).
items.problem: Corrupted leftover: a closing parenthesis with no opening one, non-standard spelling (네꺼 내꺼 for 네 거 내 거), and the content is a national generalization ('Americans keep strict accounts of what is mine and yours') that was meant as an aside to item 16. It survives in the data as a paragraph block, which GrammarLearningView never renders (only 'sentences' blocks become items, GrammarLearningView.tsx:156-167), so no learner sees it today.
items.correction: Delete the block. If the nuance of "I bought a hamburger for myself." is worth keeping, fold a neutral note into item 16's Korean parenthesis instead of a claim about a nationality.

items.locator: item 5 (items[].text, English page) — duplicate of gh2-025 item 6
items.original: Will you do me a favor?
items.problem: The identical English sentence is also gh2-025 item 6 (Korean there: "당신은 저에게 하나의 호의를 베풀어 주시겠습니까?"; here: "너는 나에게 호의를 베풀어줄래(한 가지 부탁을 들어줄래?)"). Checked against all 44 main lessons with node, this is the ONLY exactly repeated English sentence in the whole course (796 items, 795 distinct), so it reads as an accidental repeat rather than planned review.
items.correction: Keep it in one lesson and replace the other with a different 'do + 사람 + 사물' example (e.g. "Will you do me a big favor?" or "He did me a good turn."), or state explicitly that gh2-025 is a review item.

items.locator: item 20 — Korean prompt (gh2-022-1 items[].text #20) against English "I'd like to open a savings account."
items.original: 나는 저축 계정을 개설하고 싶다.
items.problem: A bank account is 계좌 in Korean; 계정 is an accounting ledger entry or an online user account (이메일 계정). "저축 계정" is not what a Korean says at a bank, so the prompt mis-teaches the meaning of the English phrase it is pairing with.
items.correction: Change to "나는 저축 예금 계좌를 개설하고 싶다." (or "보통예금 계좌를 만들고 싶습니다.").

items.original: 당신의 새해의 결심들은 무엇들인가?
items.problem: "무엇들" does not exist in Korean (무엇 has no plural form), and the doubled 의 … 의 plus 결심들 is an English-shaped calque. No natural gloss is provided for this item.
items.correction: Change to "당신의 새해 결심은 무엇입니까?"

items.original: 당신은 당신의 식사 끝났습니까?
items.problem: Ungrammatical: the object has no particle and the sentence mixes a subject (당신은) with an unmarked noun (식사) before an intransitive 끝났습니까. No natural gloss is provided.
items.correction: Change to "식사 다 하셨습니까?" (literal gloss if wanted: "당신은 식사를 끝냈습니까?").

items.locator: blocks[] paragraph block between item 4 and item 5 (Korean page)
items.original: 상관하시겠습니까(싫어하시겠습니까? 괜찮겠습니까)?
items.problem: An orphaned gloss for item 4's "Would you mind …?" left in a paragraph block, which is never rendered. As written it is also a fragment that reads as a separate question rather than as a note on 'mind'.
items.correction: Delete the block, or merge the useful part into item 4's Korean prompt (e.g. "… 질문을 해도 괜찮으시겠습니까? (mind = 꺼리다)").

items.locator: item 6 — Korean prompt (gh2-024-1 items[].text #6) against English "Can you speak up, please?"
items.original: 당신은 크게 말할 수 있습니까?
items.problem: The prompt is a bare ability question with no politeness marker, while the model answer contains "please" and the phrasal verb "speak up", and the item has no alternatives. Measured with the shipped grader: the fully correct "Can you speak up?" scores only partial (70) because "please" is missing, and the faithful rendering of the Korean, "Can you speak loudly?", scores incorrect (0). Every other 'please' item in this scope (gh2-018 #24, gh2-019 #13/#23/#25, gh2-023 #14) does carry a politeness marker in the Korean.
items.correction: Change the Korean to "좀 더 크게 말씀해 주시겠습니까? (안 들려요)" and add the alternatives "Can you speak up?" and "Could you speak up, please?"

items.locator: gh2-025-1 item n="11" (English gh2-025 item 11 = "I'll take that one over there.")
items.original: 나는 저 너머에 저것을 사겠다.
items.problem: 'over there' means 저기에 (있는), not 저 너머에 (= beyond that / on the far side). As written the Korean is also ungrammatical as a noun phrase — 저 너머에 저것을 does not modify 저것 — so the prompt reads as a broken sentence rather than 'that one over there'.
items.correction: "나는 저기에 있는 저것을 사겠다. (저기 저걸로 할게요.)"

items.locator: gh2-025-1 item n="19"; same wording in gh2-026-1 item n="3" ("이 환급 전표에 서명하고…")
items.original: 저는 이것에 대한 환급을 받고 싶습니다.
items.problem: For returning a purchase to a shop, Korean uses 환불; 환급 is used for tax, insurance or overpayment refunds. Both of these items are shop-counter situations (items 19-20 of lesson 25 and item 3 of lesson 26 are about a defective product and a refund check).
items.correction: gh2-025-1 #19 → "저는 이것에 대한 환불을 받고 싶습니다."; gh2-026-1 #3 → "이 환불 전표에 서명하고 그것을 출납계원에게 가져가라."

items.locator: gh2-026 item n="8" / gh2-026-1 item n="8"
items.original: Would he mind if I ask him to direct me to the station?
items.problem: The polite pattern pairs 'would … mind' with a past-form if-clause (Would he mind if I asked …), while the present-form if-clause pairs with 'do/does … mind' (Does he mind if I ask …). Mixing 'Would' with 'ask' is the form English grammar references explicitly correct. In a grammar course this models a broken conditional, and because no alternative is listed, a learner who writes the standard "Would he mind if I asked him to direct me to the station?" gets only partial credit (70 of 100) — 'ask'/'asked' is edit distance 1, so the grader returns 'partial', not 'exact' (map §5.1).
items.correction: Change the model answer to "Would he mind if I asked him to direct me to the station?" and add "Does he mind if I ask him to direct me to the station?" as an alternative.

items.original: 그것 근처에서 가장 유명한 건물은 무엇입니까?
items.problem: The English model answer is "What's the most prominent building near it?" — in this context (asking for directions, right after the landmark question) 'prominent' means 눈에 잘 띄는 / 두드러진, not 유명한. 유명한 is 'famous'. The item has no alternatives, and per the shipped grader (map §5.1) 'famous' against 'prominent' is neither a function-word pair nor looksLikeSameWord, so the natural answer "What's the most famous building near it?" is graded incorrect = 0 points.
items.correction: Change the Korean prompt to "그것 근처에서 가장 눈에 잘 띄는 (두드러진) 건물은 무엇입니까?", and/or add "What's the most famous building near it?" to alternatives.

items.locator: gh2-027 blocks[2] (paragraph) and gh2-027-1 blocks[2] (paragraph), between items 12 and 13
items.original: { "type": "paragraph", "text": "he'll get better grades maybe even straight A's next year." }  (Korean pair: "어쩌면 심지어 “올 에이”까지 받을 것으로 확신한다.")
items.problem: A leftover sentence fragment from the 2026-09-17 merge fix sits between the two sentences blocks on both the English and the Korean page. It duplicates part of item 12 in lower case with no subject clause, it is dead data, and because it splits the sentences array in two, the top 전체 듣기 player — which reads only the FIRST sentences block (src/app/[course]/[lesson]/page.tsx:482-485) — queues only 12 of the 16 sentences. Items 13-16 of this lesson are never played by the full-lesson player. (Same root cause as map S-1; recorded here because the defective data lives in this lesson's content files.)
items.correction: Delete blocks[2] from gh2-027.json and gh2-027-1.json and merge the two remaining sentences blocks into one, so items 13-16 are in the first block. If the 'straight A's' wording is wanted, fold it into item 12 instead of leaving a stray paragraph.

items.original: 당신은 무슨 학년 안에 있습니까(몇 학년입니까?)
items.problem: Punctuation and spacing slips in displayed Korean prompts: (a) gh2-027-1 #11 has no question mark after 있습니까 and no space before the parenthesis; (b) gh2-027-1 #16 "우리 별도의 계산서를 가질 수 있습니까? 따로따로 계산할 수 있습니까?" puts the gloss as a second free-standing question instead of in parentheses like every other item, so it reads as two separate questions; (c) gh2-028-1 #10 "…(태생은)한국인이지만 시민권에 의해서는 (국적은)미국인이다." has no space after the closing parentheses; (d) gh2-033-1 #4 "너는 갈 것을 선택했다.(가는 쪽을 택했다)." has a period both before and after the parenthesis.
items.correction: (a) "당신은 무슨 학년 안에 있습니까? (몇 학년입니까?)"; (b) "우리 별도의 계산서를 가질 수 있습니까? (따로따로 계산할 수 있습니까?)"; (c) "…(태생은) 한국인이지만 시민권에 의해서는 (국적은) 미국인이다."; (d) "너는 갈 것을 선택했다. (가는 쪽을 택했다.)"

items.locator: gh2-029 item n="3" / gh2-029-1 item n="3"
items.original: 만일 누가 조지 브라운에 대하여 물으면 그를 나에게로 안내해 주세요.
items.problem: 'ask for someone' means to say you want to see or speak to that person (조지 브라운을 찾으면), not to ask ABOUT them. The Korean ~에 대하여 물으면 renders 'asks about George Brown', which changes the meaning of the whole sentence (the second clause 'direct him to me' only makes sense if the caller/visitor is looking for the person).
items.correction: "만일 누가 조지 브라운을 찾으면 그를 나에게로 안내해 주세요."

items.original: Operator, I'd like to call New York, collect.  /  I'd like to know a phone number in Seoul, Korea.
items.problem: Both model answers use 'I'd', and the shipped grader deliberately never expands 'd (grammarGrading.ts:43-45, map §5.4/S-4). Neither item lists an uncontracted alternative, so the perfectly correct "I would like to call New York, collect." / "I would like to know a phone number in Seoul, Korea." are graded 'partial' = 70 points instead of 100. Since the grader will not be changed ('d is ambiguous between would and had), the fix belongs in the content.
items.correction: Add alternatives "Operator, I would like to call New York, collect." (item 7) and "I would like to know a phone number in Seoul, Korea." (item 8).

items.locator: gh2-030 item n="2" / gh2-030-1 item n="2"
items.original: Not to pretend to know is good.
items.problem: A negated bare to-infinitive as sentence subject is extremely unnatural in modern English; native speakers say "It is good not to pretend to know." Unlike items 1/3, which pair a bare-infinitive subject with its 'It is …' counterpart, item 2 has no counterpart and no alternatives, so the learner cannot tell which structure the Korean 아는 척 하지 않는 것이 좋다 is asking for. The natural answer (7 words vs the 6-word model) exceeds the grader's 1.15× length ceiling and is graded incorrect = 0.
items.correction: Add the alternative "It is good not to pretend to know." (and "It's good not to pretend to know."); consider making that the model answer and keeping the infinitive-subject form as the alternative.

items.original: 그가 그의 나이 많은 아버지를 버리는 것은 너무 나쁘다.
items.problem: The Korean prompt says 너무 나쁘다 (= very bad), which is the wording of the ALTERNATIVE answer ("It is very bad of him to desert his old father."), not of the model answer "It is cruel of him to desert his old father." Nothing in the prompt cues 'cruel' (잔인하다). The model answer card and the Step 3 shadowing text both show the 'cruel' sentence, so the learner is shown a Korean-English pair whose key adjective does not match.
items.correction: Change the Korean prompt to "그가 그의 나이 많은 아버지를 버리는 것은 잔인하다." and keep "It is very bad of him…" as the alternative (or move 'very bad' to the model answer and 'cruel' to the alternative, so prompt and model agree).

items.original: I didn't know with whom to go.
items.problem: The Korean prompt 나는 누구와 함께 갈지 몰랐다 gives no signal of the formal pied-piped form. The everyday equivalent "I didn't know who to go with." is 7 words against the 6-word model after contraction expansion, which exceeds the grader's 1.15× word ceiling, so it is graded incorrect = 0 (map §5.1). No alternatives are listed.
items.correction: Add alternatives "I didn't know who to go with." and "I didn't know whom to go with."

items.locator: gh2-032 item n="4" / gh2-032-1 item n="4"
items.original: Three Asian concerns agreed to pay more than one million dollars in fines.
items.problem: 'concern' in the sense of a business firm is a formal, largely dated newspaper usage, and the Korean prompt is the ordinary word 회사들. The item has no alternatives, so the obvious and correct answer "Three Asian companies agreed to pay more than one million dollars in fines." is graded incorrect (0): 'companies' vs 'concerns' is not a function-word pair and fails looksLikeSameWord (map §5.1). Nothing in the prompt can lead a learner to 'concerns'.
items.correction: Add alternatives "Three Asian companies agreed to pay more than one million dollars in fines." and "Three Asian firms agreed to pay more than one million dollars in fines."; optionally make 'companies' the model answer and keep 'concerns' as the alternative.

items.original: Care to leave a message?
items.problem: The model answer is a clipped colloquialism (ellipsis of 'Would you care to…'), but the Korean prompt 메시지를 남겨놓고 싶으십니까? is a full polite question that maps to the standard "Would you like to leave a message?" — the phrasing this very lesson uses in item 8 ("Would you like to leave your name and phone number?"). With no alternatives listed, the standard answer is 7 words against a 5-word model, which exceeds the grader's 1.15× length ceiling and is graded incorrect = 0 (map §5.1).
items.correction: Add alternatives "Would you care to leave a message?" and "Would you like to leave a message?", or change the prompt to signal the clipped form, e.g. "메시지 남기시겠어요? (짧게 줄인 표현)".

items.locator: gh2-033-1 item n="9"; same problem in gh2-032-1 item n="12" ("…제발 그가 725-1081로 걸게 해라.")
items.original: 제발 그에게 조지가 전화했다고 말해주십시오.
items.problem: 제발 means 'I beg you / for heaven's sake' and is far too strong for the ordinary polite 'please' of "Please tell him George called." The same course translates 'please' correctly elsewhere (gh2-029-1 #3 uses 해 주세요), so this is an inconsistency, not a house style: 제발 appears in only 4 of the 44 Korean pages.
items.correction: gh2-033-1 #9 → "그에게 조지가 전화했다고 전해주십시오."; gh2-032-1 #12 → "…그에게 725-1081로 전화해 달라고 해 주세요."

items.locator: items[5] (n="5"), against gh2-034 items[5] "Give me a minute to change."
items.original: "나에게 옷을 갈아입을 1분을 다오."
items.problem: "a minute" here is the idiomatic "a moment", not a measured 60 seconds. Rendering it as 1분 both misstates the idiom and steers the learner to write "one minute", which the grader (no numeral/article normalisation) will not score as exact.
items.correction: Change the Korean to "옷 갈아입게 잠깐만 시간을 다오." and add the alternative "Give me a moment to change."

items.original: "담배 산업 중역들은 그들의 제품이 중독성이라는 그들의 지식을 숨길 것을 모색했다."
items.problem: 중독성 is a noun, so 중독성이라는 means "that (it) is called addictiveness"; the grammatical form is 중독성이 있다는. The rest is heavy calque (그들의 … 그들의 …, 숨길 것을 모색했다) for what is simply 숨기려 했다.
items.correction: Rewrite as "담배 회사 중역들은 자사 제품에 중독성이 있다는 사실을 알고도 이를 숨기려 했다."

items.locator: items[13] (n="13"), against gh2-034 items[13] "I'll tell you when."
items.original: "내가 너에게 그때를 말해 주겠다."
items.problem: The English is an elliptical answer to #12 ("Where should I get off to go to the station?") — "I'll tell you when (to get off)", i.e. the 의문사 + to부정사 ellipsis this lesson drills. The Korean 그때를 말해 주겠다 ("I'll tell you the time") loses both the ellipsis and the link to #12, and gives no clue that the answer must be four words ending in a bare "when". With no alternatives, every plausible faithful translation (I'll tell you the time / I'll tell you when it is) scores 0.
items.correction: Change the Korean to "(언제 내려야 하는지) 내가 너에게 말해 주겠다." and add alternatives "I will tell you when." and "I'll tell you when to get off."

items.original: KO: "이곳은 그가 그 소식을 발표하기에는 나쁜 장소이다."  /  EN: "This is the wrong place for him to announce the news." (alternatives: "This is a wrong place for him to announce the news.")
items.problem: The Korean says 나쁜 장소 (a bad place); the model answer says "the wrong place". A learner translating faithfully writes "a bad place" and is graded incorrect. Separately, the 2026-09-17 fix G2-43 changed the model answer from "a wrong place" to "the wrong place" but left the rejected form "a wrong place" sitting in alternatives, so the non-standard collocation is still shipped as a full-credit answer.
items.correction: Change the Korean to "이곳은 그가 그 소식을 발표하기에 적절하지 않은 장소이다." (or 잘못된 장소) so it matches "the wrong place", and delete the alternative "This is a wrong place for him to announce the news." (the residue of G2-43).

items.original: "The spread of AIDS prompted men to search for younger sex partners."  /  KO: "에이즈의 확산은 남성들이 더 젊은 섹스 파트너를 찾도록 충동했다."
items.problem: An unattributed, undated sweeping claim about "men" presented as plain fact. It derives from 1990s reporting on a specific regional belief (that younger partners are less likely to be infected), and without that context it reads as a general statement about male behaviour. The 2026-09-17 review already removed a sexual-violence example from this course as inappropriate for the STUDENT audience (G2-35); this item is the same class and was not reviewed.
items.correction: Replace with a neutral sentence that drills the same prompt + object + to-infinitive pattern, e.g. "The spread of AIDS prompted governments to launch education campaigns." / "에이즈의 확산은 각국 정부가 교육 캠페인을 시작하도록 촉발했다." Regenerate the speech clip after the text change.

items.original: "몇몇 주들은 흡연 관련 질병에 대한 의료 보호 비용을 되찾기 위하여 담배 회사들을 고소하고 있다."
items.problem: 고소 is a criminal complaint filed with the police or prosecution. The US state actions against tobacco companies to recover Medicaid costs were civil suits, which in Korean is (민사) 소송을 제기하다 / 제소하다. Using 고소 mislabels the legal action.
items.correction: Change to "몇몇 주들은 흡연 관련 질병에 대한 의료 보호 비용을 되찾기 위하여 담배 회사들을 상대로 소송을 제기하고 있다."

items.original: "그는 그 불신임 동의안을 무산시키기에 충분한 국회표를 장악한다."
items.problem: 국회표 is not a Korean word; parliamentary votes is 의회 표 / 국회 의원들의 표. 장악한다 in the plain present is also an unnatural rendering of "controls" here — Korean would use 확보하고 있다.
items.correction: Change to "그는 그 불신임 동의안을 무산시키기에 충분한 의회 표를 확보하고 있다."

items.original: "He cannot be poor to buy the car."  /  KO: "그 차를 사다니 그는 가난할 리가 없다."
items.problem: Two problems. (1) The Korean 사다니 refers to a purchase that has already happened, so the ground clause needs the perfect infinitive — the lesson's own #4 uses exactly that pattern ("He must have been rich to marry her."), so the file is internally inconsistent. (2) After an adjective, "to buy" is read by default as purpose ("too poor to buy"), so "He cannot be poor to buy the car" reads as nonsense ("he must not be poor in order to buy the car") rather than as a judgement. The judgement frame is idiomatic with must be, not with cannot be + adjective.
items.correction: Use "He cannot be poor if he bought that car." as the model answer, or keep the infinitive drill with "He cannot be poor to have bought that car." Add the other as an alternative. Regenerate the speech clip after the text change.

items.original: "A man to raise the fund must be employed."  /  KO: "그 기금을 모금할 사람이 고용되어야 한다."
items.problem: The Korean says 사람 (person), but the English says "a man" — a gendered narrowing the prompt does not ask for, and one modern ELT material avoids. "raise the fund" is also off: one raises funds or raises money for a fund.
items.correction: Change to "Someone to raise the funds must be hired." and keep "A man to raise the fund must be employed." as an alternative so existing learners are not penalised. Regenerate the speech clip after the text change.

items.original: EN: "The president might use his constitutional power to dismiss the parliament."  /  KO: "그 대통령은 그의 헌법상의 권한을 사용하여 그 의회를 해산시킬지 모른다. (의회를 해산시키기 위하여 헌법상의 권한을 사용할지 모른다.)"
items.problem: The Korean says 해산 (dissolve), but the English says "dismiss". The constitutional term for ending a parliament's term is dissolve; dismiss is used for a government, cabinet or prime minister, not for the legislature. The English is therefore both an inaccurate rendering of the Korean prompt and imprecise terminology, and there is no alternative, so a learner who correctly writes "dissolve" scores 0.
items.correction: Change the model answer to "The president might use his constitutional power to dissolve the parliament." and, if leniency is wanted, add "The president might use his constitutional power to dissolve parliament." as an alternative. Regenerate the speech clip after the text change.

items.original: "이 쥬스는 네가 마실 것이다."
items.problem: 쥬스 is a pre-standard transliteration; the 외래어 표기법 form is 주스. The same file already uses modern forms elsewhere, so this is an isolated leftover.
items.correction: Change to "이 주스는 네가 마실 것이다."

items.locator: items[13] (n="13") alternatives[0], plus gh2-037-1 items[13] Korean prompt
items.original: "text": "I'd like to have a phone installed in my apartment.", "alternatives": ["I'd like to have my phone disconnected in my apartment."]  /  KO: "나는 나의 아파트에 전화가 설치되게(끊어지게) 하고 싶다."
items.problem: The accepted alternative means the OPPOSITE of the model answer (install vs disconnect), so gradeAgainstReferences gives full marks to a sentence that says the reverse of what the item teaches. The Korean prompt itself offers two contradictory glosses, 설치되게 (installed) and 끊어지게 (disconnected), so the learner cannot know which one is being asked for. This is the same defect class the 2026-09-17 review caught as G2-30 (gh2-029 #12), but this instance was missed. Also "have my phone disconnected in my apartment" is unidiomatic — the place adjunct is redundant with "my phone".
items.correction: Delete the alternative "I'd like to have my phone disconnected in my apartment." and delete "(끊어지게)" from the Korean prompt so it reads "나는 나의 아파트에 전화가 설치되게 하고 싶다." If a second useful alternative is wanted, add "I would like to have a phone installed in my apartment." (the grader does not expand 'd — see map S-4, which already lists gh2-037#13).

items.original: KO: "나는 약간의 수정이 만들어지게 했다. (고치게 했다.)"  /  EN: "I had a little alteration made."
items.problem: In the clothing context set by #14–#15 (custom-tailored suit, bought off the rack), alteration is 수선, not 수정. 수정 means correcting or revising a text or a plan; a Korean speaker would never call taking in a suit 수정. The rest of the gloss, 수정이 만들어지게 했다, is also a word-for-word calque of "made" rather than Korean.
items.correction: Change the Korean to "나는 약간의 수선을 맡겼다. (옷을 조금 고치게 했다.)"

items.original: "Who is the girl to sing?"  /  KO: "노래할 소녀는 누구인가?(누가 노래할 소녀인가?)"
items.problem: A bare to-infinitive modifying the complement of a wh-question ("the girl to sing") is not used this way in English; "to sing" after "the girl" is read as purpose or as a missing object ("the girl to sing to"). The intended meaning (the girl who is going to sing) needs a relative clause or a be-to construction. The paired item #18 ("Who is the girl studying in my study?") uses a participle and is fine, which shows the contrast the lesson wants can be made without an unidiomatic model.
items.correction: Change to "Who is the girl who is going to sing?" and add alternatives "Who is the girl that is to sing?" and "Who is the girl going to sing?". Regenerate the speech clip after the text change.

items.original: "He put off going to Pusan."  /  KO: "그는 부산에 가는 것을 연기했다."
items.problem: "Pusan" is the pre-2000 McCune–Reischauer romanization. The official Revised Romanization, in use since 2000 and the form on every Korean road sign, passport and ticket, is "Busan". The item has no alternatives, so a learner who writes the current official spelling is graded incorrect. The same lesson's #9 was already corrected to the Revised form ("Gyeongsang-do") by G2-45, so the file is internally inconsistent.
items.correction: Change the model answer to "He put off going to Busan." and add "He put off going to Pusan." as an alternative for older learners. Regenerate the Azure Ava clip after the text change (the clip key hashes the English text).

items.locator: items[13] and items[14] (n="13", "14"); same wording in gh2-040-1 items[5]
items.original: "당신은 저 너머에 서있는 그 숙녀를 압니까?" / "당신은 그 소년이 저 너머에 서있는 것을 보았습니까?"
items.problem: 저 너머 means beyond/on the far side of something, not "over there"; the natural gloss of over there is 저기에 / 저쪽에. Also 서있는 should be spaced 서 있는 (본용언 + 보조용언).
items.correction: Change both to "저쪽에 서 있는" (…그 숙녀를 압니까? / …그 소년이 저쪽에 서 있는 것을 보았습니까?), and fix the same 저 너머에서 in gh2-040-1 #5.

items.locator: items[4] (n="4"), against gh2-039 items[4] "Let's give it a try."
items.original: "그것에게 시식을 주자(그것을 시식해보자)."
items.problem: Two errors. (1) 그것에게 is the animate dative — it cannot take an inanimate object, so "그것에게 시식을 주자" is not grammatical Korean; it is a word-for-word calque of give + it + a try. (2) 시식 means sampling food (as at a supermarket tasting stand), not trying/attempting. "Give it a try" is 한번 해 보자 / 한번 가 보자. In the surrounding restaurant dialogue (#3 a newly opened Korean restaurant, #5 I'm buying) the sense is "let's try that place".
items.correction: Replace the Korean with "한번 가 보자(한번 시도해 보자)."

items.original: "내가 사고 있다(내가 산다)."
items.problem: "I'm buying." here is the fixed idiom meaning "it's on me / I'll pay", which in Korean is 내가 낼게 / 내가 살게. The primary gloss 내가 사고 있다 is a literal present-progressive ("I am in the middle of purchasing something") and is not a sentence a Korean speaker would say; the file's own parenthetical 내가 산다 already shows the intended sense, which makes the primary gloss plainly wrong.
items.correction: Replace the Korean with "내가 낼게(내가 살게)."

items.original: "그의 자녀들이 열심히 공부하는(일하는) 어머니는 행복하다."
items.problem: The antecedent is 어머니 (whose children), so the possessive must be 그녀의 / 자기; 그의 refers to a male. The English is "The mother whose children work hard is happy."
items.correction: Change to "자기 자녀들이 열심히 공부하는(일하는) 어머니는 행복하다."

items.original: "당신이 보고 있는 그 조각들은 걸작품 들이다."
items.problem: Stray space before the plural suffix — 걸작품 들이다 must be 걸작품들이다. This is the same PDF-linebreak residue class the previous audit fixed as G2-21/G2-44 in other lessons, and it was missed here.
items.correction: Change to "당신이 보고 있는 그 조각들은 걸작품들이다."

items.original: "There are rumours that this government is collapsing."
items.problem: British spelling in a course that is otherwise American (Medicaid, the U.S., coin-op laundries, brown-bag it). The item has no alternatives and the grader does not normalise spelling, so a learner who writes the American "rumors" — the spelling Korean schools teach — is graded incorrect. The 2026-09-17 review flagged this class as G2-22 and the lesson table lists gh2-040 under G2-22, but the alternative was never added.
items.correction: Change the model answer to "There are rumors that this government is collapsing." and add "There are rumours that this government is collapsing." as an alternative (or keep the British form as the model and add the American one). Regenerate the speech clip if the model text changes.

items.original: "미국에는 동전으로 작동하는 세탁기와 드라이어가 있는 많은 동전으로 작동하는 세탁소들이 있다."
items.problem: 동전으로 작동하는 appears twice in one sentence, producing a prompt that is painful to read and that gives away nothing about the relative-clause structure being drilled. 세탁소 also means a shop where staff wash or dry-clean for you; a self-service coin-op laundry is 빨래방 / 코인 세탁소 in Korean.
items.correction: Change to "미국에는 동전으로 작동하는 세탁기와 건조기를 갖춘 빨래방이 많이 있다."

items.original: "그 게임에는 그것이 없으면 그것을 할 수 없는 몇 가지 기본 규칙들이있다."
items.problem: Missing space: 규칙들이있다 must be 규칙들이 있다. Same PDF residue class as G2-21/G2-44, missed here.
items.correction: Change to "그 게임에는 그것이 없으면 그것을 할 수 없는 몇 가지 기본 규칙들이 있다."

items.original: "나는 전기와 개스가 켜지기를(꺼지기를) 원한다."
items.problem: 개스 is a pre-standard transliteration; the 외래어 표기법 form is 가스. (The contradictory parenthetical 꺼지기를 is covered by the separate High finding on this item.)
items.correction: Change to "나는 전기와 가스가 켜지기를 원한다."

items.original: KO: "그 공격은 시위를 벌이는 코카잎재배자들을 지지해서였다 (지원하기 위해서였다)."  /  EN: "The attacks were in support of coca leaf growers who staged demonstrations."
items.problem: The English relative clause is past ("who staged demonstrations"); the Korean uses the present 시위를 벌이는, so the learner is steered to "who stage demonstrations". 코카잎재배자들 is also run together and should be spaced 코카 잎 재배자들.
items.correction: Change to "그 공격은 시위를 벌인 코카 잎 재배자들을 지지하기 위한 것이었다."

items.original: "Why this is a problem was dramatically illustrated when keynoter Susan was ousted as a former marijuana user."  /  KO: "이것이 왜 문제인가 하는 것은 기조 연설자 수전이 이전에 마리화나를 사용했다는 이유로 쫓겨났을 때 극적으로 드러났다."
items.problem: Two problems remain after the G2-38 truncation fix. (1) "keynoter Susan" gives a journalistic title with a bare first name and no surname, which reads as truncated source text and leaves the sentence about no identifiable person. (2) "ousted as a former marijuana user" is unidiomatic — ousted as X normally means removed from the role of X, so this literally says she was removed from the post of former marijuana user. The Korean correctly says 이유로 (because of), which the English does not express, so the faithful translation ("because she was a former marijuana user") scores 0.
items.correction: Rewrite the English as "Why this is a problem was dramatically illustrated when the keynote speaker was ousted for having been a marijuana user." and align the Korean ("…기조 연설자가 과거 마리화나 사용자였다는 이유로 쫓겨났을 때…"). If a real named case is intended, restore the full name from the source. Regenerate the speech clip after the text change.

items.locator: blocks[2] (the paragraph block between the two sentences blocks)
items.original: { "type": "paragraph", "text": "마리화나 사용자로서 축출되었을 때 극적으로 나타났다." }
items.problem: Orphaned residue of the 2026-09-17 G2-38 fix: the tail of item #8's Korean was merged back into the item, but the old fragment was left behind as a standalone paragraph block, splitting the Korean sentences into 8 + 4. It is dead data (GrammarLearningView flattens only sentences blocks, so item alignment is unaffected), but it still duplicates part of #8 and will mislead the next person who edits this file. Already listed in docs/qa-2026-09-18/maps/grammar2.md §2.4; recorded here because it sits in a file in this scope and is still unfixed.
items.correction: Delete blocks[2] from gh2-042-1.json so the file has a single sentences block of 12 items, the same shape as gh2-042.json. (The other nine files listed in map §2.4 need the same treatment, but they are outside this scope.)

items.original: 친절하지 않는 소녀가 없었다.
items.problem: Korean conjugation error. 친절하다 is a descriptive verb (형용사), so its negated adnominal form is 친절하지 않은, not 친절하지 않는 (-는 is for action verbs). The topic particle would also read better than 가 in a negative-existential sentence.
items.correction: "친절하지 않은 소녀는 없었다." Korean-side only, no clip impact.

items.original: It is natural that you be disappointed at not passing the exam.
items.problem: "natural" is an emotive/evaluative adjective, not one of the mandative triggers (essential, vital, crucial, imperative…). After "It is natural that…" standard English uses putative *should* (BrE: "It is natural that you should be disappointed") or the plain indicative ("It is natural that you are disappointed"); the bare subjunctive "that you be" is at best marginal here. Neither standard form is in `alternatives`, and I measured both against the shipped grader: "It is natural that you should be disappointed at not passing the exam." → **partial** (70/100), and "It is natural that you are disappointed at not passing the exam." → **partial** (70/100).
items.correction: Add both to `alternatives`: "It is natural that you should be disappointed at not passing the exam." and "It is natural that you are disappointed at not passing the exam." Changing the primary `text` would delete this sentence's Azure-Ava clip, so adding alternatives is the cheap fix; if the primary is changed, regenerate with `node scripts/generate-azure-ava.mjs`.

items.original: 당신이 우연히 이 동네에 있게 되면 우리 집에 들리세요.
items.problem: 들리다 means "to be heard / to be lifted". The verb for "drop by" is 들르다, whose 해요체 imperative is 들르세요. 들리세요 is one of the most-cited spelling mistakes in Korean.
items.correction: "당신이 우연히 이 동네에 있게 되면 우리 집에 들르세요." Korean-side only, no clip impact.

items.original: Political analysts are just as convinced that Clinton will beat Dole as they were that Reagan would beat Mondale.   [KO: "정치 분석가들은 레이건이 먼데일을 무찌를 것이라고 확신했던 것과 똑같이 클린턴이 돌을 무찌를 것이라고 확신한다."]
items.problem: The sentence is grammatically fine and both facts are true (Clinton beat Dole in 1996, Reagan beat Mondale in 1984), but it is written in the present tense — "analysts **are** convinced that Clinton **will** beat Dole" — so it presents a thirty-year-old election as a live race. Compounding this, the Korean renders Dole as 돌, which a Korean reader parses first as the noun "stone", giving "클린턴이 돌을 무찌를 것" ≈ "Clinton will defeat a stone".
items.correction: Either leave the English alone (changing it deletes the clip) and disambiguate on the Korean side — "…클린턴이 (밥) 돌 후보를 무찌를 것이라고 확신한다" — or, if the sentence is refreshed, keep the same as…as structure with names a 2026 learner recognises and regenerate the clip with `node scripts/generate-azure-ava.mjs`.

items.original: Put back the book where you found it.
items.problem: With a following "where…" clause, the natural and overwhelmingly commoner English is "Put the book back where you found it." The stored order invites the reading that "where you found it" modifies "the book" rather than the verb. That natural form is not in `alternatives`: I measured it against the shipped grader and "Put the book back where you found it." grades **partial** (70/100).
items.correction: Add "Put the book back where you found it." to this item's `alternatives`. (Leaving the primary `text` alone keeps the existing voice clip.)

items.original: 그는 나에게 자신이 영어를 잘 말할 수 있는 방법을(어떻게 영어를 잘 말할 수 있는지)보여주었다.
items.problem: Missing space after the closing parenthesis: "…있는지)보여주었다". Every other parenthetical gloss in this course puts a space there (compare #9 in the same file, "…없는가)이다", which closes a sentence, and gh2-047-1 #16 "…믿었다).").
items.correction: "…(어떻게 영어를 잘 말할 수 있는지) 보여주었다." Korean-side only, no clip impact.

items.original: 이것이 내가 당신과 동의할 수 없는 이유(왜 당신과 동의할 수 없는가)이다.
items.problem: 동의하다 takes 에/에게 in Korean (의견에 동의하다, 당신에게 동의하다). "당신과 동의하다" is a word-for-word carry-over of the English preposition "with" and is not natural Korean.
items.correction: "이것이 내가 당신의 의견에 동의할 수 없는 이유(왜 당신에게 동의할 수 없는가)이다." Korean-side only, no clip impact.

items.locator: gh2-045.json blocks[2] — leftover `paragraph` block between the two `sentences` blocks
items.original: { "type": "paragraph", "text": "never found out." }
items.problem: This is an orphaned tail fragment of an alternative wording of item 1 ("The exact time when the murder had been committed was never discovered / never found out."). It is not rendered, but it splits the item list into two `sentences` blocks (1 item | 14 items), and the page's top 전체 듣기 player reads only the FIRST `sentences` block. The lesson therefore queues 1 clip for 15 sentences — 14 of the 15 sentences of this lesson can never be played from the top player. gh2-045 has the worst ratio of any lesson in the course.
items.correction: Delete blocks[2] and merge the two `sentences` blocks into one so all 15 items sit in a single block. If the alternative wording is worth keeping, put it in item 1's `alternatives` as "The exact time when the murder had been committed was never found out." instead of leaving it as loose prose.

items.original: { "type": "paragraph", "text": "you at the station." }
items.problem: Orphaned tail fragment of item #3 ("…so that I can meet you at the station."). Not rendered, but it splits the item list into 3 + 11, and the top 전체 듣기 player reads only the first `sentences` block, so the lesson queues 3 clips for 14 sentences: 11 sentences have no full-lesson playback.
items.correction: Delete blocks[2] and merge the two `sentences` blocks into one.

items.original: He used to come here last year.
items.problem: `alternatives` are not just a grading allowance — GrammarLearningView.tsx renders them to the learner as "다른 정답: …" (:917) and "(또는: …)" (:1267). "used to" is normally used without a definite past time point; a bounded, specific frame like "last year" is exactly the combination Korean grammar references and exam keys mark wrong ("used to" + last year / yesterday). The item already has a correct second alternative, "He would often come here last year.", which covers the past-habit reading, so this one adds nothing but risk.
items.correction: Remove "He used to come here last year." from `alternatives`, or replace it with "He used to come here." if a `used to` form is wanted. Deleting an alternative does not touch any clip.

items.original: 24명 이상의 선원이 살해되고 35명이 더 부상당했다.
items.problem: The English is "More than 24 seamen were killed and 35 more were wounded." — sailors killed in an attack. 살해되다 means specifically *to be murdered* and is the wrong register for combat or accident deaths; Korean uses 사망하다 / 숨지다 (or 전사하다 for military deaths) here. The 부상당했다 half of the sentence already shows the intended register.
items.correction: "24명이 넘는 선원이 사망하고 35명이 더 부상당했다." Korean-side only, no clip impact.

items.original: 여기에서는 신용카드가 존중됩니까(신용카드 받습니까)?
items.problem: "honor" in "Are credit cards honored here?" means *accept / take as valid payment*, not 존중하다 (respect). The headline Korean 존중됩니까 is a dictionary-first-sense mistranslation; only the parenthetical gloss carries the real meaning. Since the learner writes English FROM this Korean, the prompt as written points at "Are credit cards respected here?".
items.correction: Make the accepted sense the headline and keep the literal gloss second: "여기에서 신용카드를 받습니까(신용카드가 통용됩니까)?" — Korean-side only, so no voice clip is affected.

items.original: 너는 이것을 하지 말았어야 한다. (이러지 않아도 되는데, 이렇게 까지 하지 않아도 되는데.)
items.problem: Spacing error: 까지 is an auxiliary particle (보조사) and attaches to the preceding word, so it is written 이렇게까지, not 이렇게 까지.
items.correction: "…(이러지 않아도 되는데, 이렇게까지 하지 않아도 되는데.)" Korean-side only, no clip impact.

items.original: 나는 이것이 공식 파티가 아니면 좋겠다.
items.problem: The English is "I wish this were not a formal party." A "formal party" is a dress-code party (격식을 차리는 / 정장 차림의 파티). 공식 파티 means an *official* party (an organisation's official function), which is a different thing and is normally rendered "official party" in English.
items.correction: "나는 이것이 격식을 차리는 파티(정장 파티)가 아니면 좋겠다." — Korean-side only, no clip impact.

items.locator: gh2-048.json blocks[2], blocks[4], blocks[6] — three leftover `paragraph` blocks
items.original: blocks[2]: "I would have given you a ring."  /  blocks[4]: "they would have had food and clothes."  /  blocks[6]: "they could not have been contaminated by the HIV virus."
items.problem: Three orphaned tail fragments of alternative wordings of items #3, #9 and #11. Not rendered, but they split the item list into 3 | 6 | 2 | 5, and the top 전체 듣기 player reads only the first block: 3 clips for 16 sentences, so 13 sentences have no full-lesson playback. Note also that blocks[6] contains "the HIV virus", a redundancy (HIV already ends in "virus") that should not be revived if these fragments are ever promoted into `alternatives`.
items.correction: Delete blocks[2], [4] and [6] and merge the four `sentences` blocks into one. If any of the three wordings is worth keeping, add it to the matching item's `alternatives` as a complete sentence, with "contaminated with HIV" rather than "contaminated by the HIV virus".

items.locator: gh2-049-1.json blocks[1].items[0] and items[2] — Korean prompts #1 and #3
items.original: #1: "그는 나에게“나는 당신에게 한 사과를 빚지고 있다(사과할 것이 있다)”라고 말했다."  /  #3: "그는“당신은 100달러 지폐를 받습니까?”라고 물을 것이다."
items.problem: Missing space before the opening quotation mark. I checked every curly-quoted prompt in this lesson and gh2-050-1 with node: #1 and #3 have a Hangul syllable immediately before “ (게, 는), while #5, #7, #9, #11, #13 of the same file and #1, #3, #5, #7 of gh2-050-1 all have a space. So these two are the outliers, not the convention.
items.correction: "그는 나에게 “나는 …" and "그는 “당신은 …" — add the space in both. Korean-side only, no clip impact.

items.locator: gh2-049-1.json blocks[1].items[6] and items[7] — Korean prompts #7 and #8
items.original: #7: "그 은행 출납계원은 “이 은행의 계정을 갖는 것이 좋을 것입니다.”라고 말했다."  /  #8: "그 은행 출납계원은 내가 그 은행의 계정을 가질 것을 권했다."
items.problem: A bank account is 계좌 in Korean. 계정 is the word for an online/service account (Google 계정, 이메일 계정) and is also an accounting-ledger term; it is not what a bank teller offers. Both prompts in this bank-counter pair use the wrong noun.
items.correction: Replace 계정 with 계좌 in both: "…이 은행의 계좌를 갖는(만드는) 것이 좋을 것입니다." and "…그 은행의 계좌를 가질 것을 권했다." Korean-side only, no clip impact.

items.locator: gh2-049.json blocks[1].items[9] — English model answer #10 and its alternatives[0]
items.original: "text": "She said that it was a little something for me for my graduation.", "alternatives": ["She said that was a little something for me on my graduation."]
items.problem: This is the indirect-speech partner of #9, "This is a little something for you on your graduation.", and the Korean prompts of #9 and #10 both use 졸업에 대하여. The mechanical conversion a learner is being taught to perform is therefore "She said that it was a little something for me **on** my graduation." — but the model answer silently switches the preposition to *for*, and the single alternative changes a different thing (it drops "it"). I measured the expected answer against the shipped grader: "She said that it was a little something for me on my graduation." grades **partial** (70/100).
items.correction: Add "She said that it was a little something for me on my graduation." to `alternatives` (keeping the existing entries). Adding alternatives touches no English `text`, so no clip is lost.

items.locator: gh2-049.json blocks[1].items[12] and items[13] — #13 and #14 (and the matching Korean prompts in gh2-049-1.json)
items.original: #13: "Lincoln said, \"Honesty is the best policy.\""  /  #14: "Lincoln said that honesty is the best policy."
items.problem: There is no reliable record of Lincoln saying this. The proverb first appears in English in Sir Edwin Sandys, *Europae Speculum* (1599) — "Our grosse conceipts, who think honestie the best policie" — and was popularised in America by Benjamin Franklin in *Poor Richard's Almanack*. The grammar point (a general truth keeps the present tense after a past reporting verb) works with any speaker, so the misattribution buys nothing.
items.correction: Keep the pattern, drop the false attribution — e.g. "My teacher said, \"Honesty is the best policy.\"" / "My teacher said that honesty is the best policy.", or attribute it correctly to Franklin. NOTE: either version changes the English `text` of two items, so regenerate their clips in the same commit with `node scripts/generate-azure-ava.mjs`. If the owner prefers not to touch the clips, the cheapest fix is a Korean-side note on gh2-049-1 #13 saying the saying is a proverb, not a Lincoln quotation.

items.original: 일본의 관리들은 제약 회사들을 경쟁으로부터 보호하는 것에 골몰한 나머지(모색해서) 혈우병 환자들 사이에 HIV가 퍼지는 것을 막지 못했다.
items.problem: Two problems in one prompt. (a) The stray "(모색해서)" is an un-deleted second rendering of "sought to" sitting inside the sentence — the reader meets two competing verbs, 골몰한 나머지 and 모색해서, with nothing to say which to use. (b) 골몰한 나머지 ("so absorbed in … that") adds a causal/excessive nuance that "sought to protect … , failing to prevent …" does not have; the English is a simple participial result clause. This is the longest and hardest item in the lesson and the only one the learner cannot parse cleanly.
items.correction: "일본의 관리들은 제약 회사들을 경쟁으로부터 보호하려 했고, 그 결과 혈우병 환자들 사이에 HIV가 퍼지는 것을 막지 못했다." Korean-side only, no clip impact.

items.locator: gh2-050-1.json blocks[4] and blocks[5] — leftover Korean `paragraph` blocks
items.original: blocks[4]: "열처리되지 않은 혈액 제품의 판매를 방지하지 안았는데 그것이 1800명 이상의"  /  blocks[5]: "혈우병자들의 에이즈균 감염의 결과를 가져왔다."  (blocks[2]: "받아들였다는 것을 안다.")
items.problem: The Korean counterparts of the gh2-050 leftovers. Beyond being orphaned, they carry two content errors that must not be revived if anyone ever merges them back: "방지하지 안았는데" should be 않았는데 (안다/않다 confusion), and "에이즈균" calls HIV a 균 (a germ/bacterium) when it is a virus — the right Korean is HIV 감염 or 에이즈 바이러스.
items.correction: Delete blocks[2], [4] and [5] together with their English counterparts in gh2-050.json (see the gh2-050 corruption finding). Do not promote this text into an item; if any of it is wanted, rewrite it as "…판매를 막지 않았고, 그 결과 1,800명이 넘는 혈우병 환자가 HIV에 감염되었다."

items.locator: gh2-050.json blocks[2], blocks[4], blocks[5] — three leftover `paragraph` blocks
items.original: blocks[2]: "Washington."  /  blocks[4]: "sale of unheated blood products, which resulted in the HIV infection of more than 1,800"  /  blocks[5]: "hemophiliacs."
items.problem: Orphaned fragments: blocks[2] is the tail of item #9, and blocks[4]+[5] together are the tail of the ORIGINAL item #10, which read "…failing to prevent the sale of unheated blood products, which resulted in the HIV infection of more than 1,800 hemophiliacs." The stored item #10 is now a shortened rewrite ("failing to prevent the spread of HIV among hemophiliacs"), so the file ships two different versions of the same sentence. Structurally the blocks split the item list 9 | 1, and the top 전체 듣기 player reads only the first block: the final sentence of the final lesson of the course never plays.
items.correction: Delete blocks[2], [4] and [5] and merge the two `sentences` blocks into one, so all 10 items are in one block and item #10 plays. Keep the current (shorter) item #10 text and its matching Korean — changing the English would delete its Azure-Ava clip and require `node scripts/generate-azure-ava.mjs`.

items.original: { "ko": "그것은 기쁩니다", "en": "It's a pleasure" }
items.problem: "그것은 기쁩니다" is not grammatical Korean: 기쁘다 describes a person's feeling, so an inanimate 그것 cannot 기쁘다. It is a word-by-word gloss of the dummy subject "it". The lesson's own Korean paragraph renders the same clause naturally ("오늘 당신과 함께 있어 정말 기쁩니다."). The English side also uses a straight apostrophe ("It's") while sentence #2 uses the curly one ("It’s").
items.correction: ko "정말 기쁩니다" ↔ en "It’s a pleasure" (drop 그것은, and match the apostrophe used in the sentence).

items.original: 나의 이름은 홍길동입니다 그리고 나는 서울에 삽니다.
items.problem: Two independent clauses are run together with no punctuation after 홍길동입니다, so the Korean sentence is not correctly written.
items.correction: 나의 이름은 홍길동이고, 나는 서울에 삽니다. (or 나의 이름은 홍길동입니다. 그리고 나는 서울에 삽니다.)

items.original: 나는 나의 친구들 주위에 있기를 좋아하고 그들도 제 주위에 있기를 좋아합니다.
items.problem: The speech level changes inside one sentence: it starts with the plain 나는/나의 and ends with the humble 제. Paragraph #5 of the same lesson also switches to 저 ("대부분의 사람들이 저를 좋아합니다.") while #1-#4 use 나.
items.correction: Keep one register across the lesson, e.g. "저는 제 친구들과 함께 있는 것을 좋아하고, 친구들도 저와 함께 있는 것을 좋아합니다."

items.original: { "ko": "나는 내 친구들 주위에 있기를 좋아합니다", "en": "I love to be around my friends," }
items.problem: The drill list starts with sentence #3 and only then gives the three chunks of sentence #1, so working down the list practises the lesson's sentences out of order. Separately, chunkDrills[3] "그러나 나는 약간의 부끄러움을 탑니다." ↔ "but I am also a little shy" drops the "also" (또한) that the sentence and the Korean paragraph both carry.
items.correction: Order the drills sentence #1 first ("I am a very outgoing person," / "but I am also a little shy" / "around new people."), then sentence #3; and change ko to "그러나 나는 또한 약간 부끄러움을 탑니다".

items.locator: blocks paragraph #2 (KO for sentence #2) and chunkDrills[3]
items.original: 저는 많은 사람들 가운데서 이야기하는 것을 두려워하지만, 모든 사람들은 제가 마음에 드는 사람이고 함께 있으면 재미있는 사람이라고 합니다.  /  { "ko": "많은 사람들 가운데서 이야기하는 것을", "en": "to talk a lot around people," }
items.problem: The English is "Even though I am afraid to talk a lot around people" — "a lot" modifies the talking. The Korean moves "a lot" onto the people ("많은 사람들 가운데서" = among many people) and drops it from the verb, so the Korean says "afraid to talk among many people", a different claim about a shy person. The chunk drill repeats the same wrong mapping, teaching 많은 사람들 = "a lot ... people". The Korean also drops the "very" of "a very likable person" (the drill has 매우).
items.correction: 저는 사람들 앞에서 말을 많이 하는 것을 두려워하지만, 모든 사람들은 제가 매우 호감 가는 사람이고 함께 있으면 재미있는 사람이라고 합니다. / drill ko "사람들 앞에서 말을 많이 하는 것을".

items.original: 나의 취미들은 책 읽기, 음악듣기, 등산, 영화보기, 스포츠에 참가하는 것 입니다.
items.problem: Korean spacing errors: "음악듣기" → "음악 듣기", "영화보기" → "영화 보기", "것 입니다" → "것입니다". Paragraph #3, "나는 컴퓨터게임 하기도 또한 좋아합니다.", doubles the "also" (…하기도 + 또한) and writes "컴퓨터게임" without a space.
items.correction: 나의 취미는 책 읽기, 음악 듣기, 등산, 영화 보기, 스포츠 참여입니다. / 나는 컴퓨터 게임 하기도 좋아합니다.

items.original: EN "I have been studying English for (3, 4 or 5) years so far." / KO "나는 지금까지 3~5년 동안 영어를 공부해오고 있습니다."
items.problem: The English parentheses are a pick-one blank for the learner's own number; the Korean turns them into a range, "3~5년" (three to five years), which is a different statement, and it drops the blank markers the course uses everywhere else (s1-2 keeps "(10)살"). The lesson's own drill has it right: "지금까지 (3, 4 또는 5)년 동안".
items.correction: 나는 지금까지 (3, 4 또는 5)년 동안 영어를 공부해 오고 있습니다.

items.original: 당신에게 저의 가족을 소개할 수 있는 기회를 주셔서 감사합니다.
items.problem: The whole point of this two-line lesson is two different ways to say the same thing: #1 "Thank you for the chance to tell you about my family." and #2 "Thank you for this opportunity to introduce my family." Both Korean paragraphs, however, use 소개하다, so paragraph #1 and paragraph #2 ("저의 가족을 소개할 수 있는 기회를 주셔서 감사합니다.") are effectively the same sentence, and the "tell you about" wording is never translated. The lesson's own drill has the right wording: "나의 가족에 대해 당신에게 말할".
items.correction: 저의 가족에 대해 말씀드릴 수 있는 기회를 주셔서 감사합니다.

items.original: 저의 가족은 (4) 명 입니다: 저의 아버지, 어머니, 여동생, 그리고 저 자신입니다.
items.problem: "(4) 명 입니다" must be written "(4)명입니다", and the sentence closes twice (…입니다: …입니다) because the English colon was carried over into Korean, which does not use it this way.
items.correction: 저의 가족은 (4)명입니다. 저의 아버지, 어머니, 여동생 그리고 저입니다.

items.original: { "ko": "나의 아버지, 나의 어머니, 나의 누나 그리고 나 자신", "en": "my father, my mother, my sister, and myself." }
items.problem: The same "my sister" is 여동생 (younger sister) in the Korean paragraph but 누나 in the drill. 누나 is an older sister and can only be used by a male speaker, so the two Korean texts of one lesson describe different families, and chapter 2 elsewhere (s2-5, s2-6) consistently says 여동생. The drill is also an orphan: there is no chunk for "There are (4) people in my family:", so the list starts mid-sentence.
items.correction: ko "나의 아버지, 나의 어머니, 나의 여동생 그리고 나 자신", and add ko "저의 가족은 (4)명입니다" ↔ en "There are (4) people in my family:" in front of it.

items.original: { "ko": "하나 또는 그이상의 남동생이나 여동생을", "en": "one more brother or sister." }
items.problem: "하나 또는 그 이상의" means "one or more", not "one more". The lesson's own Korean paragraph is correct ("남동생이나 여동생이 한 명 더 있으면 좋겠습니다"), so the drill contradicts it and mis-teaches the phrase "one more". "그이상" is also missing the space (그 이상).
items.correction: ko "남동생이나 여동생을 한 명 더".

items.original: { "ko": "거의 약 십년 동안", "en": "for almost ten years." }
items.problem: "거의 약" doubles the approximation (almost + about) for a plain "almost ten years", and "십년" needs a space (십 년). chunkDrills[2] "수 년동안" has the spaces in the wrong places (should be 수년 동안), and paragraph #6 "그녀는 세상에서 최고의 어머니 이십니다." must be written "어머니이십니다".
items.correction: drill ko "거의 십 년 동안"; drill ko "수년 동안"; paragraph #6 "그녀는 세상에서 최고의 어머니이십니다."

items.original: 나의 어머니는 훌륭한 요리사 이시고 여전히 아름다운 여성 이십니다.
items.problem: "요리사 이시고" and "여성 이십니다" must be written "요리사이시고" / "여성이십니다". "a very good cook" is also flattened to "훌륭한 요리사", which reads as an occupation (the previous lesson says the mother is 가정주부), and the "very" disappears. The lesson also switches honorifics between neighbouring lines ("도와줍니다" in #4 vs "가십니다" in #5; "그분들은 … 되어줬습니다" in #3), and #1 calls the sister "나의 동생" while chunkDrills[2] calls her "나의 누이".
items.correction: 나의 어머니는 요리를 아주 잘하시고, 여전히 아름다운 여성이십니다. (and make the honorific level and the word for the sister consistent across the lesson)

items.original: { "ko": "집안일을", "en": "around the house." }
items.problem: This tail fragment of sentence #4 sits at the very top of the drill list, six entries before its own main clause (chunkDrills[6] "나의 아버지는 항상 잘 도와주십니다 / My father is always helpful"), so the list opens with a stranded prepositional phrase. The pair itself is also wrong: 집안일을 is an object marked with 을 ("housework"), while "around the house" is a place phrase, so nothing in the Korean corresponds to the English chunk.
items.correction: Move it to directly after chunkDrills[6] and re-pair it, e.g. ko "집안에서" ↔ en "around the house.", or merge the two into one pair: ko "나의 아버지는 항상 집안일을 잘 도와주십니다" ↔ en "My father is always helpful around the house."

items.original: EN "My sister attends (School Name) Elementary School." / KO "나의 여동생은 (한국)초등학교에 다닙니다."
items.problem: The English has the learner's blank "(School Name)", but the Korean fills it with a concrete name, "(한국)", instead of the blank label the course uses elsewhere (s1-2: "(학교 이름) 초등학교"). A learner working from the Korean prompt would try to say "Korea Elementary School". "(한국)초등학교" is also missing the space before 초등학교.
items.correction: 나의 여동생은 (학교 이름) 초등학교에 다닙니다.

items.original: { "ko": "그녀는 더 재능이 있습니다.", "en": "She is more talented" }
items.problem: The drill list starts with sentence #4 and then goes back to sentences #2 and #3; sentence #1 has no drill. Spacing errors in the same list: "피아노치기를" → "피아노 치기를", "모든 종류의 과목공부하기를" → "모든 종류의 과목 공부하기를", and "그녀는 잘 합니다." → "그녀는 잘합니다".
items.correction: Reorder to sentence #2 → #3 → #4 (optionally adding #1) and fix the three spacing errors.

items.locator: top-level "title" (also reproduced in the instruction block and the page h1)
items.original: "title": "Sister's School & Talents (자매의 학교와 재능)"
items.problem: 자매 means "sisters" as a pair or group of female siblings, not "my sister". The lesson is about the speaker's 여동생 (as the body text says), and a male speaker cannot be part of a 자매 at all, so the Korean gloss of the title is wrong.
items.correction: Sister's School & Talents (여동생의 학교와 재능)

items.original: 사실상 그녀는 개를 한 마리 가지고 있습니다.
items.problem: 사실상 means "in effect / virtually", not "in fact" (사실은/실제로); the lesson's own drill uses the correct "사실". "개를 … 가지고 있습니다" is also a literal calque of "has a dog" — in Korean a pet is 키우다/기르다, not 가지다.
items.correction: 사실 그녀는 개를 한 마리 키웁니다.

items.original: { "ko": "그녀는 개를 가지고 있습니다 .", "en": "she has a dog." }
items.problem: A stray space is left before the full stop ("있습니다 ."), which no other entry in the course has. In the same lesson, paragraph #3 writes "음악듣기" (should be 음악 듣기) and "이야기 하기를" (should be 이야기하기를), and chunkDrills[6] "그리고 친구와 이야기 하기를" drops both the possessive and the plural of "her friends".
items.correction: ko "그녀는 개를 한 마리 키웁니다." (no space before the period); paragraph #3 "또한 그녀는 음악 듣기를 좋아하고 전화로 친구들과 이야기하기를 좋아합니다."; chunkDrills[6] ko "그리고 그녀의 친구들과 이야기하기를".

items.locator: top-level "title" (also reproduced in the instruction block and the page h1)
items.original: "title": "Sister's Hobby (자매의 취미)"
items.problem: Same error as s2-5: 자매 means "sisters" as a pair or group, while the lesson is about the speaker's 여동생, and a male speaker cannot belong to a 자매.
items.correction: Sister's Hobby (여동생의 취미)

items.original: EN: "He/She is one of my best friends."  KO: "그는/그녀는 나의 가장 좋은 친구 중 한명 입니다."
items.problem: Two issues. (1) "best friend" is 가장 친한 친구 in Korean; 가장 좋은 친구 is a word-for-word rendering that Koreans do not use for this meaning. The very next lesson (s3-2, paragraphs 4 and 5) correctly uses 가장 친한 친구, so the course contradicts itself one page later. (2) Spacing: "한명 입니다" should be "한 명입니다" — 명 is a 의존명사 (spaced from the number) and 입니다 is a 서술격 조사 (attached to the preceding word).
items.correction: "그는/그녀는 나의 가장 친한 친구 중 한 명입니다."

items.original: EN: "He/She is an outgoing but sometimes shy person like me."  KO: "그는/그녀는 외향적이지만 나와 같이 부끄러움을 타는 사람입니다."
items.problem: The Korean drops "sometimes". The English says the friend is outgoing but *occasionally* shy; the Korean says the friend is outgoing but is a shy person like me — i.e. shy as a fixed trait. The lesson's own chunk drill renders the same clause correctly as "그러나 때때로 나처럼 내성적이기도 합니다.", so the paragraph is the odd one out. "like me" is also re-attached to "shy" only, whereas in English it modifies the whole description.
items.correction: "그는/그녀는 나처럼 외향적이지만 때때로 수줍음을 타는 사람입니다."

items.original: s3-2 #6-#7: {"ko":"나의 가장 친한 친구는 (이름)입니다.","en":"My best friend is (name),"} then {"ko":"그리고 나는 그를 알아왔습니다","en":"and I have known him/her"}  —  s4-5 #1: {"ko":"나의 큰삼촌 (삼촌 이름)입니다.","en":"is my oldest uncle, (uncle’s name)."}
items.problem: Both lessons have a sentence whose drill chain cannot rebuild it. In s3-2 the closing chunk of sentence #5, "for 3 years.", is missing, so the chain stops at "and I have known him/her" and the drill jumps to sentence #7. In s4-5 the drill set opens with a chunk that begins with the verb "is" — the subject chunk "My favorite relative" ("내가 가장 좋아하는 친척은") does not exist, so sentence #1 can never be produced from the drills.
items.correction: Add {"ko":"3년 동안","en":"for 3 years."} after s3-2 drill #7, and add {"ko":"내가 가장 좋아하는 친척은","en":"My favorite relative"} before s4-5 drill #1.

items.original: #8: {"ko":"그는 나의 친구입니다.","en":"He/She is my friend,"} and #9 {"en":"and I am proud of him/her."} appear before #10 {"en":"His/Her drawings are"} / #11 {"en":"very bright and colorful."} and #12 {"en":"So I can learn a lot"} / #13 {"en":"from him/her."}
items.problem: The drills run in the order sentence 2, 3, 7, 5, 6, 8 — sentence #7 is drilled before sentences #5 and #6, so the practice sequence does not follow the passage the learner has just read. Sentences #1 and #4 have no drills at all. Drill #9 also adds an intensifier that is not in the English: "그리고 나는 그를 매우 자랑스럽게 생각합니다." for "and I am proud of him/her." (no "very").
items.correction: Reorder the array to sentence order (2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8), add drills for sentences #1 and #4, and drop 매우 from drill #9.

items.locator: Korean paragraph 2 (also s3-2 paragraph 4, s4-3 paragraph 3, s3-1 paragraph 3)
items.original: "그는/그녀는 훌륭한 피아노 연주가 이고 아주 강한 운동선수 입니다."
items.problem: A space is inserted before the copula in several rendered Korean paragraphs: "연주가 이고" and "운동선수 입니다" here, "누가 나의 가장 친한 친구 일까요?" (s3-2 paragraph 4), "나의 아버지는 둘째 아들 입니다." (s4-3 paragraph 3), "한명 입니다" (s3-1 paragraph 3). 이다/입니다 is a 서술격 조사 and must be written attached to the noun. The same paragraph also carries the space into the chunk drills (s3-3 drills #1 and #2).
items.correction: "그는/그녀는 훌륭한 피아노 연주가이고 아주 강한 운동선수입니다." — and likewise "친구일까요?", "둘째 아들입니다.", "한 명입니다." These are Korean-only edits, so no audio clip is affected.

items.original: EN: "He/She always understands my problems, and when I need help, he/she is always there."  KO: "그는/그녀는 항상 나의 문제들을 이해해 주고 내가 도움을 필요로 할 때 그는/그녀는 항상 거기에 있습니다."
items.problem: "is always there" is an idiom meaning "is always there for me / always stands by me". Rendering it literally as "항상 거기에 있습니다" produces a Korean sentence about physical location — "he is always in that place" — which is not what the English says. "나의 문제들을" is also a Europeanised plural; Korean would simply say 내 고민을.
items.correction: "그는/그녀는 항상 내 고민을 이해해 주고, 내가 도움이 필요할 때면 늘 곁에 있어 줍니다."

items.locator: sentence #3 (and its relation to sentence #2) / Korean paragraph 3
items.original: #2: "He/She is an excellent piano player and a very strong athlete."  #3: "In addition, he/she is good at playing the piano, soccer, computer games, and he/she is good at speaking English."
items.problem: "In addition" promises new information, but the first item it lists — playing the piano — is exactly what sentence #2 just said ("an excellent piano player"). The sentence also repeats the frame "he/she is good at" twice in one sentence, and the list "the piano, soccer, computer games" has no conjunction before its last item, so it reads as unfinished. The Korean paragraph reproduces the same duplication ("피아노, 축구, 컴퓨터 게임 하기를 잘하고" right after "훌륭한 피아노 연주가").
items.correction: Drop the duplicated item and tidy the list: "In addition, he/she is good at playing soccer and computer games, and he/she speaks English well." / "게다가 그는/그녀는 축구와 컴퓨터 게임을 잘하고 영어도 잘합니다." (Requires regenerating the clip for #3.)

items.locator: Korean paragraph 1 (translation of sentence #1), compared with chunk drills #3 and #4
items.original: KO paragraph: "그는/그녀는 때때로 경찰관, 소방관, 선생님, 의사, 통역관이 되기를 원하고 지역 사회를 섬기기를 원한다고 나에게 말합니다."  drills: {"ko":"경찰관, 소방관, 선생님, 의사, 통역사가 되고 싶다고"} and {"ko":"그리고 그는 봉사하기를 원합니다."}
items.problem: Two inconsistencies inside one lesson. (1) "interpreter" is 통역관 in the rendered paragraph but 통역사 in the drill. 통역사 is the ordinary job title and is the term the course itself uses for Chapter 16 ("통역사가 되고 싶은 이유"); 통역관 is used for government/official interpreters. (2) "serve the community" is 지역 사회를 섬기기를 in the paragraph but 봉사하기를 in the drill. 섬기다 means to serve in the sense of revering or waiting on (a parent, a lord, a god) and is the wrong register here; 지역 사회에 봉사하다 is the normal collocation.
items.correction: "그는/그녀는 때때로 경찰관, 소방관, 선생님, 의사, 통역사가 되어 지역 사회에 봉사하고 싶다고 나에게 말합니다."

items.original: "He/She sometimes tells me that he/she wants to be a police officer, firefighter, teacher, doctor, interpreter, and he/she wants to serve the community."
items.problem: The five-item job list has no conjunction before its final item, so "interpreter," runs straight into "and he/she wants to serve the community". The single "and" in the sentence therefore looks like it is joining "interpreter" to "he/she wants to serve", and the list reads as cut off. This is the only sentence in the lesson and it is 30 words long, which makes the parsing problem worse.
items.correction: "He/She sometimes tells me that he/she wants to be a police officer, a firefighter, a teacher, a doctor, or an interpreter, and that he/she wants to serve the community." (Requires regenerating the clip for #1.)

items.original: #1 EN: "Let me introduce my relatives to you."  KO: "당신에게 저의 친척을 소개하고 싶습니다."  #2 KO: "나의 친척에 대해서 말씀 드리겠습니다."
items.problem: (1) "Let me introduce…" is translated with the "would like to" phrasing 소개하고 싶습니다. The course already uses that exact Korean for a different English sentence — s3-1 #2 "I would like to introduce my friend to you." = "나의 친구를 당신에게 소개하고 싶습니다." — so one Korean prompt now maps to two different English targets while "Let me…" (소개하겠습니다 / 소개해 드리겠습니다) is never taught. (2) The two adjacent sentences switch speech level: 저의 in #1, 나의 in #2.
items.correction: #1: "제 친척을 소개해 드리겠습니다."  #2: "제 친척에 대해 말씀드리겠습니다." (Korean-only edits; also note 말씀 드리겠습니다 → 말씀드리겠습니다, one word.)

items.locator: s4-3 sentence #4 + Korean paragraph 4; s4-4 sentence #4 + Korean paragraph 4
items.original: s4-3 #4: "My grandparents live with my oldest uncle." / "나의 할아버지와 할머니는 나의 큰아버지와 함께 살고 계십니다."  —  s4-4 #4: "Because my grandfather passed away several years ago, my grandmother lives with my mother’s eldest brother." / "할아버지께서 몇 년 전에 돌아가셨기 때문에 나의 할머니는 나의 어머니의 가장 큰 오빠와 살고 있습니다."
items.problem: Read in sequence, the two lessons contradict each other: in 4-3 both grandparents are alive and living with the oldest uncle, and one lesson later the grandfather 'passed away several years ago'. The intended reading is paternal grandparents in 4-3 (친가) and maternal grandparents in 4-4 (외가), but neither the English nor the Korean marks the side. English uses the bare 'my grandparents' / 'my grandfather' both times, and the Korean uses the bare '할아버지/할머니' in 4-4 where Korean has the distinct terms 외할아버지/외할머니 that would have removed the ambiguity instantly.
items.correction: Mark the side explicitly. s4-3 #4: "My father's parents live with my oldest uncle." / "친할아버지와 친할머니는 나의 큰아버지와 함께 살고 계십니다."  s4-4 #4: "Because my mother's father passed away several years ago, my mother's mother lives with my mother's eldest brother." / "외할아버지께서 몇 년 전에 돌아가셨기 때문에 외할머니는 큰외삼촌과 함께 살고 계십니다." (Changing the English requires regenerating the Azure-Ava clips for both sentences.)

items.original: s4-3 #1: "First of all, my father has (two) brothers and (two) sisters."  s4-3 #2: "My mother also has (two) brothers and (two) sisters."  s4-4 #2: "She has two older brothers and two older sisters."
items.problem: Two related inconsistencies. (1) The numbers are marked as learner blanks in s4-3 — "(two)" — but the corresponding Korean paragraphs write them as fixed facts, "두 명의 남자형제와 두 명의 여자형제", with no parentheses, so the Korean prompt tells the learner the answer is two. (2) One lesson later the same fact is hard-coded in English with no parentheses at all: s4-4 #2 "two older brothers and two older sisters". A learner who filled the s4-3 blanks with their own family's numbers is then required to say "two" in s4-4.
items.correction: Either make the numbers blanks consistently — s4-4 #2 "She has (two) older brothers and (two) older sisters." and the Korean "(두) 명의 오빠와 (두) 명의 언니" — or drop the parentheses in s4-3 and treat the whole chapter as a fixed model family.

items.locator: s4-3 Korean paragraph 4 vs s4-5 Korean paragraph 1 and s4-6 title/Korean paragraph 3
items.original: s4-3 #4 KO: "나의 할아버지와 할머니는 나의 큰아버지와 함께 살고 계십니다."  s4-5 #1 KO: "나의 가장 좋아하는 친척은 나의 큰삼촌 (삼촌 이름)입니다."  s4-6 title: "Oldest Uncle's Talents (큰삼촌의 재능)"
items.problem: The same English phrase "my oldest uncle", referring to the same person (the father's eldest brother, the one the grandparents live with), is 큰아버지 in s4-3 and 큰삼촌 in s4-5 and in the s4-6 title and paragraph. 큰아버지 is the standard term for the father's older brother; 큰삼촌 is colloquial and, for many learners, implies an unmarried uncle. Additionally, "My favorite relative" is translated "나의 가장 좋아하는 친척" — the possessive 나의 cannot govern the adverb 가장 this way; it should be 내가 가장 좋아하는 친척.
items.correction: Use one term throughout the chapter — 큰아버지 — and fix the relative clause: "내가 가장 좋아하는 친척은 나의 큰아버지 (삼촌 이름)입니다." and the s4-6 title "(큰아버지의 재능)". Korean-only edits.

items.original: "할아버지께서 몇 년 전에 돌아가셨기 때문에 나의 할머니는 나의 어머니의 가장 큰 오빠와 살고 있습니다."
items.problem: (1) "my mother's eldest brother" is rendered "나의 어머니의 가장 큰 오빠", which is not Korean — 가장 큰 오빠 reads as "the physically biggest older brother". Korean has a single word for this relative: 큰외삼촌 (or 어머니의 큰오빠). (2) The verb drops honorifics for the grandmother — 살고 있습니다 instead of 사십니다 / 살고 계십니다 — although the same course uses 살고 계십니다 for the grandparents one lesson earlier (s4-3 paragraph 4) and uses 돌아가셨기 for the grandfather in this very sentence.
items.correction: "외할아버지께서 몇 년 전에 돌아가셨기 때문에 외할머니는 큰외삼촌과 함께 살고 계십니다."

items.locator: s4-4 chunkDrill #5; s3-2 chunkDrill #12; s3-4 chunkDrills #1, #3, #5
items.original: s4-4 #5: {"ko":"나의 삼촌과 이모들은","en":"My uncles and aunts"}  —  s3-2 #12: {"ko":"그는 돌아다니기를 좋아하고","en":"He/She likes to hang out"}  —  s3-4 #1: {"ko":"그는 종종 나에게 말합니다.","en":"He/She sometimes tells me that"}, #3: {"ko":"경찰관, 소방관, 선생님, 의사, 통역사가 되고 싶다고","en":"a police officer, firefighter, teacher, doctor, interpreter,"}, #5: {"ko":"지역사회에서","en":"the community."}
items.problem: Four wrong mappings inside the drills. (1) s4-4 is the 외가 (mother's side) lesson and its own paragraph correctly says 외삼촌, but the drill says 삼촌, which names the father's brother. (2) "hang out" is 돌아다니다 ("wander around") in the drill, while the lesson's paragraph correctly uses 어울려 놀다. (3) s3-4 drill #1 renders "sometimes" as 종종 (often), although the lesson's own paragraph uses the correct 때때로. (4) s3-4 drill #3 repeats 되고 싶다고, which drill #2 ("그가 되기를 원한다고" = "he/she wants to be") has already supplied, so the Korean says it twice for one English clause; and drill #5 gives 지역사회에서 ("in the community") for the direct object "the community" (지역 사회에).
items.correction: s4-4 #5 → "나의 외삼촌들과 이모들은"; s3-2 #12 → "그는 친구들과 어울려 놀기를 좋아하고"; s3-4 #1 → "그는 때때로 나에게 말합니다."; s3-4 #3 → "경찰관, 소방관, 선생님, 의사, 통역사가"; s3-4 #5 → "지역 사회에". Korean-only edits.

items.original: EN: "When we get together we usually go out for dinner."  KO: "우리가 함께 모였을 때 우리는 종종 저녁 먹으러 밖으로 나갑니다."  drill #7: {"ko":"우리는 종종 외식하러 나갑니다.","en":"we usually go out for dinner."}
items.problem: Two errors in one sentence. (1) "usually" is rendered 종종, which means "often / now and then"; "usually" is 보통 or 대개 — a clearly higher frequency. The same 종종 is used for "sometimes" in s3-4's drill, so 종종 is doing duty for two different English adverbs. (2) The habitual present "When we get together" becomes the past 모였을 때 ("when we had gathered"); the habitual reading needs 모일 때면 or 모일 때.
items.correction: "우리가 함께 모일 때면 우리는 보통 저녁을 먹으러 나갑니다." and the same fix in the chunk drill.

items.locator: sentence #1 (and the order of sentences #1-#2 relative to #3-#5)
items.original: #1: "My other uncles are very successful, too."  (lesson title: "Oldest Uncle's Talents (큰삼촌의 재능)")
items.problem: The lesson opens with "too", which points back to something that was never said: the previous lesson (s4-5) describes the oldest uncle as the speaker's favourite relative and never calls him successful. The lesson is also titled "Oldest Uncle's Talents" but spends its first two sentences on the *other* uncles; the oldest uncle only appears in #3. The natural order is #3-#5 (the oldest uncle) followed by #1-#2 (the other uncles), which is also what makes the "too" work.
items.correction: Either reorder the sentences so the oldest uncle comes first and "My other uncles are very successful, too." follows him, or drop the dangling reference: "My other uncles are very successful as well." is not enough — the antecedent still has to exist, so reordering is the real fix.

items.locator: Korean paragraph 4 (also s3-2 paragraph 5, s4-4 paragraph 3, s5-2 paragraphs 6 vs 7, s4-1 paragraphs 1 vs 2)
items.original: "제가 학교에 가기 전에 나의 어머니께서는 나에게 용돈을 주십니다."
items.problem: The humble first person 제가 and the plain first person 나의/나에게 appear in the same sentence. The same mixing occurs elsewhere in scope: s3-2 paragraph 5 ("저의 가장 친한 친구는 (이름)이고 나는 그를/그녀를 …"), s4-4 paragraph 3 ("나의 외삼촌들과 이모들은 … 그래서 저도 또한 …"), s5-2 paragraph 6 (저는) against paragraph 7 (나는) in the same lesson, and s4-1 paragraph 1 (저의) against paragraph 2 (나의).
